title: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
paragraphs: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
What the Bible actually says about the marriage bed may confront both the legalist who invented rules God never wrote—and the spouse who has used “we’re married” to excuse what love should never do.
There are questions Christians whisper because they are afraid somebody will hear them.
This is one of them.
Maybe you have wondered about it but never dared ask your pastor.
Maybe you searched online and found two opposite worlds waiting for you.
One says almost everything between husband and wife is sinful.
The other says almost nothing can be sinful once two people are married.
One produces shame.
The other can produce license.
And somewhere between them sits a husband and wife who genuinely love Jesus, genuinely love each other, and simply want to know:
What does God actually say?
Not what somebody's grandmother said.
Not what pornography taught.
Not what secular culture celebrates.
Not what a preacher personally dislikes.
Not what social media normalizes.
What does Scripture say?
And here is where we have to be unusually careful, because Christians should never place words in God's mouth.

The Bible explicitly condemns sexual immorality and adultery. It commands faithfulness, holiness, honor, sacrificial love, and marital responsibility. Yet Scripture does not give married couples an exhaustive catalogue naming every conceivable intimate act and placing each into a column marked “permitted” or “forbidden.”
That distinction matters.
Because calling something sin when God has not called it sin is dangerous.
But using God's silence as permission to violate everything else He has said is dangerous too.
Hebrews 13:4 gives us one of the clearest boundaries:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
The Greek is striking:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos…
Marriage is to be held in honor, and the marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
The word koitē—κοίτη—literally refers to a bed and, in this context, carries the intimate sense of the marriage bed.
But notice something Christians sometimes miss.
The verse does not say, “Marriage makes everything automatically holy.”
It tells us to honor marriage and keep the marriage bed undefiled, while warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Marriage is sacred.
It is not a moral loophole.
A wedding ring does not turn sin into righteousness.
At the same time, neither should Christians invent commandments that Scripture itself never gives.
That is where wisdom begins.
The question is therefore bigger than, “Does the Bible mention this particular act by name?”
We also have to ask:
Does this honor the covenant?
Does this involve another person, physically or through cultivated sexual infidelity?
Does it feed lust directed outside the marriage?
Does it violate holiness?
Does it degrade my spouse?
Does it cause harm?
Is there coercion, intimidation, manipulation, humiliation, or fear?
Can husband and wife approach this with a clear conscience before Christ?
Does it express covenant love—or merely use another person's body to satisfy selfish desire?
Those questions matter because Christian sexual ethics are not merely about anatomy.
They are about worship.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “fornication” in the KJV is porneia—πορνεία—a broad New Testament term for sexual immorality.
Notice Paul's destination:
Sanctification.
Holiness.
God is not merely interested in where your body has been.
He is interested in what your desires are becoming.
Jesus drove that truth all the way into the heart when He confronted adultery of the heart. Sexual purity cannot be reduced to the technical defense, “But I never physically cheated.”
You can remain physically beside your spouse while allowing your imagination to become unfaithful.
You can bring another person into your marriage without that person ever walking through your bedroom door.
A screen can do it.
Pornography can do it.
Secret fantasies deliberately cultivated around someone else can do it.
Comparison can do it.
An emotional or sexual fixation outside your covenant can begin turning the person God gave you into a substitute for somebody living inside your imagination.
And suddenly the question is no longer simply:
“What acts are allowed?”
The more frightening question becomes:
“Who is actually present in my heart when I touch my spouse?”
Jesus does not merely want outward technical compliance.
He wants truth in the inward person.
Then Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that was astonishingly reciprocal in its wording.
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

Then Paul deliberately mirrors the language in both directions: the wife does not possess unilateral authority over her body, and neither does the husband over his. He follows that reciprocal statement by saying that spouses should not deprive one another except temporarily and by agreement for prayer.
The Greek phrase in verse 5 is revealing:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
Together.
The word is related to the idea from which we get “symphony”—voices sounding together.
Do not twist this passage into a weapon.
Paul is not handing one spouse a divine permission slip to force the other.
The grammar is reciprocal.
The obligations are reciprocal.
The giving is reciprocal.
Even temporary abstinence in the circumstance Paul describes is ek symphōnou—by mutual agreement.
Christian marriage therefore cannot transform coercion into love merely because vows were once spoken at an altar.
A spouse is not property.
A spouse is a person made in God's image.

If someone is frightened, pressured, threatened, deliberately hurt, degraded against his or her will, manipulated with Scripture, or told, “God says you owe me this, so you cannot say no,” something has gone terribly wrong.
Do not baptize selfishness with Bible verses.
And husbands especially need to hear the standard Scripture places before them.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is Ephesians 5:25.
Look carefully at the direction of Christlike love.
Christ “gave himself up.”
The husband modeled after Jesus is not asking, “How much can I get?”
He is learning to ask, “How faithfully can I love?”
He does not use strength to frighten.
He uses strength to serve.
He does not weaponize authority.
He lays himself down.
He does not make his wife's vulnerability dangerous.
He protects it.
Ephesians continues by telling husbands to love their wives as their own bodies.
That destroys the theology of sexual selfishness.
If your pleasure requires your spouse's terror, something is wrong.
If your satisfaction depends upon your spouse feeling degraded, something is wrong.
If you are deliberately causing injury, something is wrong.
If pornography has become the scriptwriter of your marriage, something is wrong.
If another person is being brought into the sexual covenant, adultery and sexual immorality do not become righteous because husband and wife agreed to redefine marriage.
Consent matters profoundly.
But mutual consent is not the only category in Christian ethics.
Two people can mutually agree to something God has forbidden.
Agreement cannot sanctify adultery.
Agreement cannot turn pornography into purity.
Agreement cannot make exploitation holy.
Agreement cannot make idolatry worship.
And agreement cannot overrule Christ.
Jesus remains Lord of the bedroom too.
But now we must turn the blade in the other direction.
Some Christians have suffered beneath unnecessary shame because somebody taught personal preference as though it were Scripture.
This also must stop.

If Scripture does not explicitly identify a particular act between husband and wife as sinful, we should be cautious about announcing, “God forbids this,” merely because we personally find it strange, culturally unfamiliar, or uncomfortable.
Christians do not possess legislative authority over God's conscience.
Where God has spoken, obey Him.
Where biblical principles clearly apply, apply them faithfully.
Where Scripture has not specifically spoken, do not manufacture a verse that does not exist.
This is why the better question for many married Christians is not simply:
“Where is the verse forbidding this exact thing?”
Ask something deeper.
Can we thank God for this?
Can we approach it without violating either conscience?
Is it mutually welcomed rather than pressured?
Does it preserve exclusivity?
Does it honor rather than degrade?
Does it protect rather than injure?
Does it strengthen intimacy rather than train us to objectify one another?
Is pornography or another person's image necessary to make it desirable?
Does either spouse secretly feel used afterward?
Would bringing this honestly before Christ fill us with peace—or make us desperately search for theological loopholes?
And perhaps the most revealing question:
Does this resemble the character of Jesus?
Because Christianity is not fundamentally about discovering the maximum amount of behavior we can technically defend.
It is about becoming like Christ.
That changes everything.
Suddenly sex is no longer a consumer transaction.
It becomes covenant intimacy.
Not “What can I extract from you?”
But “How can I love you?”
Not performance.
Presence.
Not comparison.
Faithfulness.
Not coercion.
Tenderness.
Not secret resentment.
Honesty.
Not pornographic imitation.
Covenant reality.
Not shame.
Grace.
And perhaps this article is hurting because your story is already complicated.
Maybe pornography entered your marriage years ago.
Maybe you pressured your spouse.
Maybe you agreed to things because you were terrified that saying no would make your spouse leave.
Maybe somebody taught you that being a “good Christian wife” meant never having boundaries.
Maybe somebody taught you that being a husband gave you ownership rather than responsibility.
Maybe you crossed lines.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe your marriage bed became cold.
Maybe intimacy became transactional.
Maybe there are memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you are reading this beside the very person you wounded.
And now shame is whispering:
Too late.
Look at what you became.
Look at what you did.
God must be disgusted with you.
But shame has forgotten the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come only for people with clean histories.
He came for sinners.
The cross is not God's monument to people who never became sexually broken.
It is God's declaration that sin is so serious Christ had to die—and grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly did.
Repentance does not mean pretending nothing happened.
It means bringing what happened into the light.
Naming sin as sin.
Ending what must end.
Confessing what must be confessed.
Seeking forgiveness.
Accepting appropriate boundaries and consequences.
Getting wise pastoral and professional help where trauma, coercion, abuse, addiction, or betrayal are involved.
And turning toward Jesus.
Not toward better hiding.
Toward Jesus.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Your scandal is your identity.”
The Gospel says, “Your sin is real—but Jesus Christ is greater.”
This is why our heartbeat remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.

He rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, calling sinners to repentance, carrying sin to a bloody cross, rising from the grave, forgiving those who trust Him, and beginning the long work of making broken people new.
Maybe your marriage needs that grace tonight.
Not another argument about who is right.
Not another secret browser window.
Not another demand.
Not another night pretending everything is fine.
Maybe it begins with two terrifyingly simple sentences:
“I haven't loved you like Christ.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And perhaps another:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It may be the first honest thing your heart has said in years.
So, are there sexual acts between husband and wife that Scripture explicitly forbids?

Scripture clearly forbids sexual immorality and adultery and commands holiness, marital faithfulness, honor, Christlike love, and reciprocal marital responsibility. It does not hand us an exhaustive catalogue naming every conceivable intimate act. Therefore we must neither invent prohibitions God did not give nor use biblical silence to excuse conduct that violates what He plainly commanded. Hebrews commands that marriage be honored and its bed remain undefiled; Paul calls believers away from porneia toward sanctification; 1 Corinthians presents marital intimacy in profoundly reciprocal language; and Ephesians places Christ's self-giving love over the marriage covenant.
The Christian question is ultimately not:
“How close can we get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
It is:
“How can our marriage—including our most private life—belong completely to Jesus?”
That question changes a bedroom.
It changes a husband.
It changes a wife.
It can change a marriage.
And Christ can change the people inside it.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your private life. But you can make one honest confession of need.
There is no shame in admitting that you need the mercy of Jesus.
Not because everybody needs to know their private story—but because somebody scrolling tonight may desperately need to discover that biblical holiness and biblical grace are not enemies.
These are conversations worth returning to slowly, prayerfully, with an open Bible.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers—and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about real human brokenness—to follow as well.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, there is another way you can help this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
But voluntary financial support is a real and biblical way believers can participate in Gospel work.
But the greatest reason to support Gospel ministry is not merchandise.
It is people.
Somewhere tonight, someone is hiding.
Someone thinks sexual sin has disqualified them forever.
Someone's marriage is bleeding behind smiling Facebook photographs.
Someone is wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them after what they have done.
Someone needs truth strong enough to confront them...
and grace strong enough to keep them from running away afterward.
If supporting Gospel Warrior helps us reach that person, then your generosity becomes more than support for content.
It helps carry a message.
Tag wisely.
Save what you need to revisit.
Follow so truth remains close.
But above everything else...
Come back to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you were wrong about something in the bedroom.
The greatest tragedy would be defending your desires so fiercely that you refused the Savior who came to transform your heart.

And the greatest miracle may begin when the door closes, the excuses stop, the secrets come into the light, and two broken people discover that Jesus Christ is still standing there with enough truth to expose them...
and enough grace to rebuild them.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the pen is surrendered to Christ.
